Independent analytic inverse-dose check and benchmark bisection described in rationale
correctness.rationale: Variation of constants gives D_s(t)=g(t) before s and g(t)−min(Delta,g(s))exp(−b(t−s)) after it. The untreated sag peaks uniquely at t_c, with g''(t_c)=−abM. For 0<s<=t_c and positive dose, the post-pulse curve has its unique maximum after t_c: writing A=1+exp(bs)min(Delta,g(s))/K, the peak occurs at t_c+log(A)/(b−a) with height M A^(−a/(b−a)). Its height strictly decreases with s before t_c since exp(bs)min(Delta,g(s)) is the minimum of two strictly increasing functions there. The upstream supremum g(s) strictly increases to M. The continuous maxima cross once, giving strict global minimax; s=0 and s>=t_c have risk M, since g(0)=0 and the upstream limit is included. Full reset gives post-peak M exp(−as), yielding exactly s_star and Delta_star, with the crossing strictly before t_c. For s in [s_star,t_c) the pulse actually required for balancing is K exp(−bs)[(M/g(s))^((b−a)/a)−1]. It is strictly decreasing from Delta_star to zero and feasible (<=g(s)) precisely when g(s)>=M exp(−as). This verifies the branch, strict monotone shift and risk, and uniqueness at the critical dose; extra available dose is unused at full reset. Expanding this inverse dose formula at t_c−u and using K exp(−bt_c)=aM/(b−a) gives Delta=abM u²/2+O(u³), independently yielding both claimed asymptotics. At Delta=0 every location ties. I also checked the benchmark (a,b,L0)=(1,2,1): s_star=log(4/3), Delta_star=3/16. At Delta=0.1 put z=exp(−s); independent 65-digit decimal bisection of 20z³−20z²+7z−2 on [1/2,3/4] gives s≈0.349977832842958 and risk z−z²≈0.208096390775130, consistent with the source's stated approximations.
residual_risks: The universal proof is analytic; the numeric benchmark is only a diagnostic. Applies to zero initial deficit, one capped additive oxygen impulse, uniform rates 0<a<b, and the full half-line, not multiple sites or a risk that omits upstream deficit.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Even importing the peak formula or the first-binding principle, the power needed at a candidate in the fixed-budget problem must be shown admissible under clipping and under the same budget at all competing sites. Optimizing one fixed fraction over sites is not optimizing one fixed dose. Matching at one site does not rank other sites under the additive law. Earlier saturation in reach length and its quadratic approach are not the fixed-dose saturation or zero-dose square-root shift.

originality.rationale: Credit prior work for the oxygen-sag model, additive impulse response setting, placing cost-optimal aerators at binding deficits, and balancing the upstream value with a downstream sag in the fixed-fraction model. The supported distinct result is the exact global capped fixed-available-dose phase diagram and its weak-dose law. The active-constraint placement and the post-peak formula alone are not new. In the fractional theorem an at-site reparameterization gives the same local peak, but not equality of the two risk functions over alternative sites; the additive-dose crossing, cap feasibility threshold, and inversion at zero dose need a separate comparison.
residual_risks: Koivo–Phillips 1975 was not retrieved in full; the cited EPA 1971 placement discussion was not verified from a usable copy. A preexisting exact one-impulse dose-standard inversion under the same saturation cap could affect priority. No negative inference is drawn from access limitations.

value.rationale: A site-independent dose budget and inability to oxygenate beyond saturation are natural constraints absent from the constant-fraction formulation. The complete unique placement and risk profile distinguishes overprovision (exact no-improvement threshold) from near-zero sensitivity (a quantitative square-root movement), which can matter in using this classical baseline. The result is a mathematical benchmark, not an engineering prescription or a new general impulse-control method.
residual_risks: Not an empirical water-quality claim; finite reaches, multiple aerators, variable flow and practical costs are outside scope.
